::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Key Takeaways

- Claude Code does its best work inside a harness: a project where the tools,
  the order of the steps, and the conventions are already decided, so Claude
  executes rather than chooses. A project template hands you one ready-made.
- Claude Code is multi-language and multi-platform: it works across Stata,
  Python, R, and shell, on Windows, macOS, and Linux, in one session.
- It can take a project from first setup to a rendered deliverable: set up the
  foundations, wire the task runner, and run the whole chain.
- You describe the outcome, and Claude writes the orchestration and handles the
  platform differences, so you never hand-wire how the tools call each other.
- Work only with de-identified or synthetic data; never let Claude read raw
  participant data.
:::

## The situation

A real analysis rarely lives in one tool. You clean the data in Stata or R, make
a plot in Python, and write the report in Quarto, with a dependency manager and
a task runner holding the pieces together. Every hop has its own command and its
own way of failing, and getting the whole thing to run start to finish is a tax
you pay again on every machine and every data refresh.

## When you reach for this

- You are starting a new multi-tool project and want the plumbing set up for
  you.
- You need to re-run an analysis end to end after a data refresh.
- You are moving an analysis to a new machine, or handing it to a collaborator.

## A stack Claude can drive

The modern research project leans on a handful of tools, and each earns its
place twice over: once for your own reproducibility, and once because it gives
Claude something to hold on to.

- **[uv](../../virtualenv/python-uv.qmd)** keeps the analysis reproducible: the
  same environment rebuilds on a colleague's laptop and on yours a year from
  now.
- **[`just`](https://github.com/casey/just)** is the orchestrator: it holds
  every operation in one file instead of in people's heads, so a newcomer can
  run the analysis on day one. It also carries per-platform variants of a
  recipe, `[windows]` and `[unix]`, so one command name works on Windows, macOS
  and Linux, and neither you nor Claude has to remember which shell the machine
  expects.
- **[Stata](../../stata/index.qmd)** or **R** carries the analysis, and its
  script is the reproducible record of what happened to the data.
- **Python** covers what sits around the analysis, from reshaping data to a
  figure that is easier to draw there than in Stata.
- **[Quarto](../../quarto/index.qmd)** ties the write-up to the results,
  generating the report's tables and figures from the analysis so the numbers
  never drift out of sync.

Together they make a project reproducible end to end and portable across
machines and operating systems. They also add up to a harness: every one of them
is driven from the command line, declares what it needs in a file, and reports
what happened in a log. That gives an agent a surface to work against and, just
as important, a set of choices it does not have to make. Claude Code runs them
all in one session, reading each log and fixing what breaks as it moves from one
tool to the next---far more reliably than in a project where the steps live only
in someone's head.

## Build the harness, or take one ready-made

The point of a harness is that the decisions are already made. Which tools the
project uses, what order the analysis runs in, where data lands at each stage,
what the code should look like---Claude chooses none of it. It works inside
choices that are already fixed, and that is what makes its output predictable
enough to trust.

You can set those conventions yourself: a folder layout, one place where the
environment is declared, a named command for each stage, and a `CLAUDE.md` in
the project root recording the rules you want followed. A template is that same
work already done.

IPA publishes two public templates.
[ipa-stata-template](https://github.com/PovertyAction/ipa-stata-template) is the
fuller harness: a numbered do-file pipeline from `00_run.do` through cleaning,
analysis and figures; `data/raw` to `data/clean` to `data/final` as the path the
data takes; a `Justfile` covering every stage; the `uv` environment; a root
`CLAUDE.md`; and Claude Code skills carrying IPA's Stata coding standards and
data-cleaning checklist.
[ipa-python-template](https://github.com/PovertyAction/ipa-python-template) is a
lighter Python scaffold---the `Justfile`, the `uv` setup, and the linting and
pre-commit configuration---without the analysis structure.

Install [`just`](https://github.com/casey/just) once for your platform; each
template's README gives the command. To use a template, create your own copy on
GitHub (**Use this template → Create a new repository**), then clone it to your
machine. See [Create a repository](../../git/create-repo.qmd) and [Clone a
repository](../../git/clone-repo.qmd).

## Set up the environment

Start Claude Code in the project folder and ask it to get the project running on
your machine: create the virtual environment, install the packages the code
needs, and point the configuration at your own Stata, R, or Python installation.
Claude runs the setup, reads what fails, and fixes it until the environment is
ready. You do not need to know which tool installs what.

You are ready when the project's setup command finishes without an error.

**From a template.** Both templates put this behind one recipe,
`just get-started`. In the Stata template the machine-specific settings live in
`.env`: copy `.env-example` and set `STATA_CMD` to your Stata executable.
Confirm with `just --list`, which prints every command the project defines.

## Put each stage behind one command

Ask Claude to give every stage of the project a single named command: one to
clean the data, one to run the analysis, one to render the report. A task runner
keeps those definitions in a file that travels with the project, so the next
person runs the analysis without reconstructing it. If the project has no task
runner, ask Claude to add one and write the first few commands; if it has one,
ask Claude to extend it for your task.

This is also where Claude earns its keep on the awkward parts: it writes the
`[windows]` and `[unix]` variants a cross-platform project needs, and `just`
selects the right one at run time. You end up with orchestration you did not
have to author, and a project that behaves the same on a colleague's machine as
on yours.

**From a template.** Both ship a `Justfile` with the stages already defined, so
Claude extends a working set instead of starting from nothing. In the Stata
template the order is fixed too: `00_run.do` calls the numbered do-files in
sequence, so Claude adds to a pipeline rather than deciding what runs when.

## Run the chain end to end

With the commands in place, ask Claude to run the whole thing and hand you the
finished deliverable. It cleans the data, runs the analysis, produces the
figures, and renders the report, reading each log as it goes; when a step fails
it reads the error, fixes the cause, and re-runs.

This is the same closed loop that works for a single script, now spanning the
whole stack. You react to the finished deliverable, not to each command.

**From a template.** In the Stata template this is `just stata-run` to run the
analysis, then `just render-report <your-report.qmd>` to produce the document.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Never run on raw data

One rule holds at every step here: never let Claude read or process raw
participant data. De-identify first, or work from a synthetic sample, and never
commit data to the repository. Keep the raw files outside the project folder, or
deny that path in Claude Code's permission settings, so the boundary does not
rest on remembering to state it in a prompt. See [Prompt
safely](../use-cases.qmd#prompt-safely).
:::

## A prompt to start from

Adapt this to your project:

```text
Set this project up on my machine: create the environment, install what
the code needs, and point the configuration at my Stata install on
Windows. Then build the descriptive-statistics report end to end: clean
the data, run the analysis, and render the Quarto report. Work only from
the de-identified sample in ./data/sample, never ./data/raw. Give each
stage a single named command, read each log, and fix failures before
moving on.
```

If you started from a template, say so in the first line and name it. Claude
will use the commands the template already defines instead of inventing new
ones.

::: {.callout-note}
## At IPA

Claude is approved for **Public** and **Internal** data only: de-identify before
you connect it, never let it reach an encrypted drive such as a Cryptomator
vault directly, and follow the [IPA AI Usage
Guidelines](https://ipastorage.box.com/s/mvr67ygvz1y3v8qmgjey67lk7msmyeks).
Contact [support@poverty-action.org](mailto:support@poverty-action.org) when a
data classification is unclear.
:::
